and the first of these this service declares.

DomainOut.description:
A claimed domain, verified or not, plus what to publish while it is not.

`verification_host`/`verification_value` are computed, not stored columns — they are a
pure function of the row's own `domain` and `verification_token`
(`app.domain.verification_txt_host`/`verification_txt_value`), always in sync by
construction rather than by remembering to update a second copy.
DomainOut.title: DomainOut

email that delivers it. It is never readable again.

MemberOut.description:
A membership, plus the parts of the person a colleague may see.

Deliberately not the user row: a person exists across organizations, and one customer
has no business learning where else they work.

OrganizationDirectoryOut.description:
An organization as OpsGrids staff sees it — the operator console's read, never a
tenant's own. Deliberately narrower than `OrganizationOut`: a staff read across every
customer on the platform has no reason to carry `settings`, `tax_ids` or
`registered_address`, and the smaller the cross-tenant surface the smaller the blast
radius of a bug in it.
OrganizationDirectoryOut.title: OrganizationDirectoryOut

OrganizationMemberOut.description:
One member of an organization, as a staff operator may see it — never `MemberOut`,
the colleague-facing shape, and never a plaintext email: PII is masked by default, and
unmasking needs its own permission plus an audit row every time (CLAUDE.md), neither of
which this read is. `id` is the membership id, the same identifier the tenant-facing
member endpoints use, so a support ticket can cross-reference one.
OrganizationMemberOut.title: OrganizationMemberOut

A stranger creating an organisation and becoming its owner (ADR-0013 §3).

**No password.** The owner sets one through the reset-link flow after proving the address
receives mail; a payload with a password here would be a credential held by a service that
has no business holding one, on an address nobody has verified.
SignupIn.title: SignupIn

post.description:
**Public by design** (ADR-0013 §3): the caller has nothing yet, not even an account.

Bypass-then-narrow, the invitation route's shape with one difference. The bypass session
answers two questions it alone can — is the slug taken, is the email already somebody's —
because under the new tenant's binding the policied `organizations` table cannot show a
clash and it would surface as a unique violation. Then an id is generated, a transaction is
bound to it, and every write happens on the app role under the ordinary policy. See the
ADR for why that is narrower than running this route as the admin role.

Both clashes are a 409 with a plain sentence. An existing email is told to sign in: an
account that already exists does not get a second organisation from the sign-up form, and
"already registered" is not the enumeration oracle a login form's 404 would be, because
the very next step — the set-password email — goes to that inbox and nobody else.

409.description: That address or that email is already taken

422.description: Not a slug, not an email

429.description: Rate limited by the gateway, per client address

get.description:
The Users tab and the Users column's per-org detail (ui/backend-data-2): id, name, a
masked email, status, joined/last-active and roles by name. Unmasking is out of scope —
there is no path here that ever returns the plaintext.

Same two-credential and bypass-then-narrow shape as `get_organization_for_operator` above:
the list itself runs on the BYPASSRLS directory session (there is no tenant to bind for a
cross-tenant caller), and the read is audited in its own tenant-bound transaction afterward.
404 first, same as the detail route, so a caller cannot page an organization that does not
exist and learn something from the shape of the (empty) response instead.

post.description:
Public by design: the invitee has a token, not yet an account.

Bypass-then-narrow (ADR-0002, path 4). The caller carries no principal, so there is no
tenant to bind until the invitation itself names one. The invitation is therefore read on
the bypass session — BYPASSRLS, SELECT-only, one row of one table — purely to learn its
organization; then a tenant-scoped transaction is opened on the application role
(NOBYPASSRLS) and every write happens under policy. The bypass touches a single lookup;
the writes stay enforced.

The token is the credential, so every failure — unknown, expired, already used — returns
the same message. A distinct "expired" reply confirms to whoever is guessing that they
found a real one. All of that validation stays inside `accept_invitation` under the tenant
session, so the resolver above cannot leak that a token was real either.

get.description:
What the caller may do, so the front end can hide controls it holds no grant for.

Declared **before** `/members/{membership_id}` so `me` is never captured as a UUID
path parameter. No permission is required — every authenticated member may read their
own grants — and there is no id to ask for somebody else's: the membership looked up is
always `principal.membership_id`, the one the caller's own token names.

Computed by `selectors.get_membership_grants`, the same selector
`GET /internal/v1/memberships/{id}/grants` uses, so the two can never disagree about
what "the widest scope wins" means. This is a convenience for the browser only — every
write still checks the permission itself, server-side, regardless of what this says.

get.description:
How far behind the relay is. **Alert on `oldest_seconds`.**

A stalled relay is the platform's quietest failure. It selects, finds nothing,
logs nothing, sleeps, and loops — `attempts` never increments and `last_error`
stays null, so the process looks healthy indefinitely while the outbox grows
without bound and every consumer downstream starves.

Deliberately **not** part of readiness. A backlog is not a reason to take the
service out of rotation: refusing traffic would stop new events being written
without helping drain the ones already queued, which makes the incident worse.
This is a metric to alert on, not a health state.

Counted through the outbox engine, not the application one. The app role is
NOBYPASSRLS and this request binds no tenant, so through it `pending` would be
zero whatever the table holds — the probe that exists to expose the stall would
be wired to the same blind spot that causes it.
get.summary: Outbox depth and age — scrape this

get.description:
Route traffic on this; restart on /health.

Conflating the two restarts a healthy process that is merely waiting on a
dependency.

Only the dependencies a service actually declares are checked. A gateway owns no
tables, so asking it for a database is asking a question whose answer means nothing
— and a readiness probe that reports on something the service does not use is worse
than no probe, because it will eventually fail for a reason nobody can act on.

Reachable only on the compose `back` network (`tests/infra`'s
`test_metrics_never_routed.py` is the lint that keeps it that way) — never behind
Caddy or a gateway, the same rule `ops_monitor`'s own `/metrics` follows.

`db_pool_in_use` is always reported when this service has a database; the three
outbox gauges only when `outbox_model` is configured — same gate as `/health/outbox`,
and the same reason: an app-role connection with no tenant bound sees zero rows.
